title: I rejoiced (Psalm 121 [122])
hookLine: let us go into the house of the Lord; pray for the peace of Jerusalem

cards: Let's go. Let's go to the beach. Let's go see Grandma.
Let's go to the game. Two words, and before anyone has moved an inch, the trip has begun. Today's psalm starts right there.

Somebody in the village says, we're going up to the house of the Lord, and the psalmist's heart jumps. A few lines later, the pilgrims are standing inside the gates of the city they walked for days to reach.

teach.h: WE SHALL GO INTO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.
teach.b: It's one of the gradual psalms, a road song, and it opens with joy. In the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." First, the joy.
Nobody is forcing anybody here; going to worship is the good news, the thing to look forward to.

Its first line is the psalm verse of the old Latin entrance chant for Laetare Sunday, the Sunday of rejoicing in the middle of Lent, and it's used in the Liturgy of the Hours for feasts of Mary, who is sometimes called the house of God.
The pilgrims stand inside the gates and look around at a city built close together, where the tribes go up to praise the name of the Lord. A long road, and now: here. Third, the prayer.
The psalm turns and asks for peace: "Pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem: and abundance for them that love thee. Let peace be in thy strength: and abundance in thy towers."
The Hebrew says it more plainly: peace within thy walls. And there's a play on sounds.

Peace is shalom, Jerusalem is Yerushalayim, and the lines chime shalom, shalom, as if the city's own name held the word. Tradition has long heard it that way, though scholars aren't sure that's where the name comes from.
Today Jerusalem is holy to Jews, to Christians and to Muslims, and people of all three pray for its peace.
The psalm doesn't say whose peace. It asks for peace inside the walls, and for the ones who love the city.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 121 [122] in the Liturgy of the Hours, often at Vespers on feasts of Mary, and its first verse, Laetatus sum, is the psalm verse of the Latin entrance chant for the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

games.q: you've walked for days and you're finally standing inside Jerusalem's gates. the psalm turns to prayer. what does it ask for?
o: peace within the walls, and for those who love the city.
games.why: it asks for peace: "Pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem: and abundance for them that love thee."

practice: Picture Jerusalem: stone walls, narrow streets, people of three faiths walking past each other every morning, and hold the ones there who are grieving or afraid.

If you pray, say the psalm's line, pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem; if you don't, wish peace to the people who live there, and then to one home you know where peace is thin.

wordCard.voice: I rejoiced. The first words of a pilgrim psalm: glad to be invited into the house of the Lord, and praying for the city's peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace, wholeness, all being well; the psalm chimes it with Yerushalayim.

carryVoice: Your line: peace within thy walls. A long road, and then the gates. That's one hundred eighty-five days.
